title: Architecting DocHub — A Secure, VPC-Only Document Platform on AWS
body:
## Situation
DocHub needed to work like an internal, Google-Drive-style platform for Avenue One's real estate documents: fully private, no public endpoints, fast search, and role-based access, across roughly 200,000 documents.

## Action
She built the system on S3 for document storage with CloudFront for private distribution, DynamoDB as the metadata layer (partition key mapped directly to the S3 folder path, sort key on upload time, GSIs on transaction type and file location), and OpenSearch, VPC-only, indexing metadata only, never document content. DynamoDB Streams fed an indexer Lambda that kept OpenSearch in sync asynchronously, decoupling storage from search. All compute ran in private subnets behind a private ALB and API Gateway; Auth0 handled identity, and presigned URLs were generated per request so no client ever touched S3 credentials directly. RBAC: User (view-only), Manager (view + upload), Admin (view + upload + delete). Documents were organized in S3 by domain (assets, MLS, bulk), each split into pre-close, post-close, and processing stages. Two real constraints shaped the API design: API Gateway's 6MB payload limit and Lambda's 10MB limit, requiring request-splitting for larger uploads. Three environments (Dev, QAT, Production), provisioned via SST.

## Outcome
The platform indexed roughly 200,000 documents with metadata-only search fast enough to answer queries like "all MLS post-close transactions in Calgary uploaded by John," while every endpoint stayed private. Cold starts were not noticeable in practice.

## Learning
Metadata had to be treated as a first-class citizen, not bolted on after storage. Designing the DynamoDB schema before writing indexing code, and decoupling storage from search through an event stream instead of a synchronous write, gave the system resilience and clear responsibility boundaries. In hindsight, she'd weigh a more traditional Serverless Framework setup against SST to reduce long-term lock-in.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: designing a production, VPC-only, event-driven serverless architecture at real scale, and reasoning clearly about specific constraints (payload limits, metadata-first schema design, sync vs. async indexing). Use for: system design interviews, AWS/architecture technical-depth questions, "walk me through a system you designed," "how do you think about search at scale without exposing document content."

title: Aurora to RDS — A Cost-Driven Database Migration
body:
## Situation
MaidLink's AWS bill was $52/month, almost entirely the database. The product is in private beta — bootstrapped, low traffic, predictable load — nowhere near the scale that justifies a premium auto-scaling database. It launched on Aurora Serverless v2, the sensible choice when load is genuinely unknown: fully managed, auto-scaling, no capacity planning. A few months in, Aurora's 0.5 ACU minimum meant always-on compute — a $43/month floor with zero queries running. Not viable for a bootstrapped product at this stage.

## Action
Sindhuja evaluated every realistic alternative. DynamoDB was genuinely cheap at low traffic, but MaidLink is deep into PostgreSQL-specific features — TSRANGE columns for availability windows, the btree_gist extension, complex joins across bookings, maids, and scheduling logic. Rewriting for DynamoDB's access patterns would have taken months — ruled out. Neon and PlanetScale offered serverless Postgres with generous free tiers, but both sit outside AWS, meaning data would leave the VPC — not negotiable for a product handling customer home addresses and booking data — ruled out. RDS PostgreSQL on a t3.micro instance stayed in the same private VPC, same Postgres 15, at roughly $14/month: a fixed instance, no code changes, just a different host endpoint.

Migration ran alongside the live Aurora cluster: all 17 schema migrations replayed, every table copied with row-count verification, then one line swapped in the deploy config to point at the new endpoint.

## Outcome
Zero downtime, a three-minute cutover. $52 to $14 a month — a 70% reduction, with no feature loss and no user impact.

## Learning
Serverless databases earn their premium when load is genuinely unpredictable and spiky. At early stage, with real but predictable traffic patterns, boring and fixed is the right call — build the right thing for right now, not the thing that would matter at a scale that hasn't arrived yet.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: real architecture decision-making under a cost constraint, systematically ruling out alternatives with concrete reasons rather than picking the trendiest option, and executing a zero-downtime migration solo. Use for: AWS/database technical-depth questions, "tell me about a cost trade-off you made," "describe an infrastructure decision and why."

title: AWS NAT Gateway Cost Discovery
body:
## Situation
MaidLink's AWS bill showed EC2 charges. That made no sense — MaidLink's backend is fully serverless; there are no EC2 instances anywhere in the architecture.

## Action
Sindhuja dug into the AWS billing dashboard line by line. The charge wasn't EC2 compute — it was a NAT Gateway, billed at roughly $44 CAD/month, charged simply for existing, not for traffic volume. She traced the reason: Lambda functions inside a private VPC need a NAT Gateway to reach the public internet — for SES (email), Bedrock (AI inference), and any other external call. Without it, those Lambdas are cut off from everything outside the VPC — a structural cost of the private-VPC-Lambda pattern, not a misconfiguration.

She evaluated the one real way to eliminate it: expose Aurora directly to the internet, locked down with strict security groups instead of keeping it VPC-private. Technically workable — and rejected. An internet-facing production database wasn't a risk worth taking to save $44/month. While researching cost options instead, she found AWS Activate — startup credits and support — as a way to offset the broader AWS bill (personal spend was running ~$150 CAD/month at the time).

## Outcome
Kept the private-VPC-Lambda architecture intact — no security trade-off made for a cost saving. Used the NAT Gateway discovery as the trigger to pursue AWS Activate credits instead of weakening the architecture.

## Learning
Serverless doesn't mean free, and "no EC2" doesn't mean "no fixed cost" — network architecture carries its own always-on cost independent of traffic. The real discipline wasn't the discovery, it was resisting the easy fix: exposing Aurora to the internet would have made the bill smaller and the system worse.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: reading AWS bills line-by-line instead of accepting them, understanding why a cost exists architecturally, and holding a security line under cost pressure as a sole engineer with no one else to check the decision. Use for: AWS/serverless technical-depth questions, "tell me about a cost trade-off," "describe a time you were tempted to cut a corner and didn't."

title: Building a TOTP/HOTP Library From Scratch
body:
## Situation
Years earlier, at Paysafe, built and published an internal 2FA npm package used across product teams on the Skrill platform (PCI-DSS regulated). Wanted to build a new one for her own public portfolio, but this time from true first principles instead of generating it, going deep enough to defend every line of the algorithm cold, not just ship something that runs.

## Action
Built `@sindhujaks/totp`, a zero-dependency TypeScript implementation of TOTP/HOTP (RFC 6238 / RFC 4226), piece by piece: base32 encoding hand-rolled with no library, HMAC-based dynamic truncation, the time-step counter swap that turns HOTP into TOTP, cryptographically secure secret generation with a hard floor on key length, and verification with constant-time comparison and real replay protection.

Pushed the design past the first working version twice. First: made the library deliberately storage-agnostic. A TOTP secret can't be stored the way a password is, the server needs the real value back every time, not just a one-way hash, so encryption-at-rest has to be the caller's job, not the library's. Second: the verification loop's first draft returned as soon as it found a match inside the drift window, technically correct, but response timing could still reveal which time-step matched. Rejected "a well-known library does it this way" as a justification and rewrote it to always do the identical amount of work regardless of outcome, closing the leak instead of inheriting it.

Published it as a real public package: GitHub repo, then npm. The npm publish itself got blocked by her own account's 2FA, now enforced via a hardware security key rather than an authenticator app, since npm phased out new TOTP-based 2FA enrollment in late 2025. Used npm's newer staged-publish flow (`npm stage publish` → `npm stage approve`) built for exactly this case: a write operation that needs real proof-of-presence from a 2FA method a CLI can't ask for a typed code.

## Outcome
Live at github.com/sindhujaIBM/totp-toolkit and npmjs.com/package/@sindhujaks/totp. 22 tests passing, checked against the actual official RFC 4226 and RFC 6238 published test vectors, not just "looks right."

## Learning
"A popular library does it this way" is not a security argument. The constant-time verification loop's original shortcut was already accepted practice elsewhere; rewriting it to remove even a minor, low-value timing leak was the right call anyway, accepted elsewhere isn't the same as correct.

Tracing the algorithm by hand, byte by byte, before trusting any of it took longer than generating a working version would have. That gap is the whole point, it's the difference between having shipped something and being able to stand behind every line of it under real questioning.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: real applied cryptography depth (HMAC, constant-time comparison, timing attacks), security-first design thinking (storage boundaries, Kerckhoffs's principle in practice), and a demonstrated instinct to push back on "good enough because others do it" instead of accepting precedent uncritically. Use for: "tell me about a security-critical system you built," "describe a time you questioned an accepted practice instead of deferring to it," "how do you approach learning something you don't yet understand deeply," "tell me about applying cryptography or security principles in practice."

title: Cutting Asset Data Ingestion from 48 Hours to Under 5 Minutes
body:
## Situation
A data pipeline at Avenue One relied on cron and Astronomer (managed Airflow) jobs to populate downstream data sources, including Snowflake, from uploaded asset data. On a good day, it took 48 hours before the data was usable.

## Action
Replaced the batch cron/Astronomer scheduling with webhook-triggered API calls, invoked on demand instead of run on a fixed schedule. The more complex path — full EventBridge/SQS orchestration — was considered and deliberately set aside in favor of simple REST calls, since the real deliverable didn't require it.

## Outcome
Ingestion time dropped from 48 hours to under 5 minutes.

## Learning
Complex isn't always better. The simplest architecture that meets the actual requirement is often the right one — this was a deliberate choice to avoid over-building, not a default.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: measurable technical impact (48 hours → under 5 minutes) and architectural restraint — choosing the simple solution on purpose rather than reaching for the more sophisticated pattern by default. Use for: "tell me about a time you improved a slow process," "describe an architecture trade-off you made," AWS/data-pipeline technical-depth questions.

title: Evaluating 4 LLM Providers for HQ
body:
## Situation
Building MaidLink's AI estimator meant coordinating multiple AI tasks — photo analysis, time estimation, checklist generation — each needing a model with a different cost, privacy policy, and integration path. Sindhuja built HQ, an internal AI-powered team where every task is owned by an agent, and needed to pick a model for it.

## Action
She evaluated four providers in order. Claude Agent SDK: the architecture fit best and it's the tool she knows most, but she's on a fixed monthly plan with no API access — Claude Code runs on the plan, the SDK doesn't. Gemini: free tier, solid performance, easy to integrate — but the free tier lets Google train on submitted data, unacceptable for a system where agents handle real tasks and decisions. Ollama: fully private, no cost, runs locally — but local means no path to share, scale, or deploy elsewhere, a ceiling that would be hit quickly. Groq: free API access, no data training on the free tier, and it cleared enough of the real constraints (cost, privacy, deployability) to be the one she chose — running `llama-3.3-70b-versatile`.

## Outcome
HQ runs on Groq. No provider was perfect — Groq cleared the most blockers for this stage.

## Learning
The lesson isn't "use Groq" — it's that there's no LLM provider without a catch: cost, privacy, infrastructure, or accessibility. The job is picking the trade-offs you can actually live with for where you are right now.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: structured, criteria-based technology evaluation (cost, privacy, deployability) rather than defaulting to the most familiar or most hyped option, and comfort revisiting a decision if the provider landscape changes. Use for: AI/LLM architecture questions, "tell me about a build-vs-buy or vendor decision," "how do you evaluate new AI tools."

## Note on the record
The published post (`content/approved/sindhuja-post-004-hq-ai-agents.md`) spells the provider "Grok" — that's a typo in the public post. The actual provider is **Groq** (groq.com). Don't propagate the "Grok" spelling into new content; if the discrepancy ever needs reconciling publicly, that's a correction to make deliberately, not silently.

title: Hiring for Her Team at Avenue One — Two Solo Loops, Two Hires
body:
## Situation
Avenue One needed to fill a spot on Sindhuja's team (3-5 engineers) with a Full Stack Developer. She ran this as a solo hiring process — no committee, no one above her overruling the call.

## Action

## Outcome
Both loops resulted in a hire: Harmanjit Singh Randhawa (joined September 2024) and Masoud Benzomhou (spelling unconfirmed, joined January 2025) — both Full Stack Developers on her team.

## Learning
Not yet captured in detail — gap noted rather than invented.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)

title: Hotjar Discovery Nobody Asked Her to Run
body:
## Situation
Sindhuja noticed that at GoA stakeholder demo sessions, the GoA liaison — **Chris Astle** (confirmed by Sindhuja 2026-10-16; CastlePoint Consulting Inc. today, background spanning Alberta Research Council and Alberta Ministry of Advanced Education/Economic Development and Trade) — always ran the demos — users were never left to navigate the SkillUp platform on their own. Nobody asked her to investigate, but she suspected the liaison was covering a UX gap rather than just being helpful.

## Action
The first thing tried was an onboarding library to surface the platform's key features on first load. It didn't solve the problem. So, without waiting for approval — no sprint ticket, no approval meeting — she implemented Hotjar and watched how real users actually navigated the platform without guidance, running some A/B and user acceptance testing alongside it (specific platform/tool not recalled).

## Outcome
The combined evidence was clear: users consistently tried to filter by industry first. A single bar chart answered the most common need. Sindhuja took that evidence — Hotjar behavior plus the testing results — and recommended bringing on a UX designer. The product direction shifted, the team hired a UX designer, and the next version landed significantly better with stakeholders.

## Learning
The point wasn't that her hypothesis was right — it was that she built the evidence before anyone had to ask for it, and she didn't stop at the first fix attempt (the onboarding library) when it didn't work.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: customer discovery instinct, taking initiative without a mandate, and letting real usage data (not opinion) drive a product decision. Use for: "give an example of initiative," "tell me about a UX/product discovery you ran," questions probing product sense in a technical leader.

title: I Inherited a Codebase Nobody Could Run
body:
## Business Problem
Avenue One was paying roughly $50K–75K a year for Box, so Transaction Manager and Property Management could store real estate documents from across the deal lifecycle: title and closing paperwork, leasing documents, renovation records, inspection reports. An engineer had already started building DocHub, meant to run on S3 for a few dollars a month instead, using Claude to generate most of the system. He left before it was usable, and without transferring meaningful knowledge of how it worked.

## Customer Problem
Internal stakeholders across the deal lifecycle needed DocHub to keep working, and needed confidence that whoever took it over actually understood their existing structure and access patterns, not just the code.

## Technical Architecture
React frontend, SST-based serverless AWS infrastructure, S3 for document storage, Lambda functions, API Gateway. Access control was later redesigned into 3-tier RBAC via Auth0 (see [[rbac-redesign]]). Full system design captured separately in [[dochub-architecture-deep-dive]].

## Technologies
React, SST (Serverless Stack), AWS Lambda, S3, API Gateway, Auth0, Claude (used by the original engineer to generate most of the codebase, and by Sindhuja during her own rebuild).

## Trade-offs
Not yet captured in detail, gap noted rather than invented.

## Challenges
Her manager handed her the system with an offhand "well, give it to Sindhu" in a meeting. There was no documentation, no running state, no ERDs, no deployment notes. The codebase had numerous unused Lambda functions scattered through it, left over from AI-generated iterations built without architectural review. There was also an invisible dependency: another team's pod was already relying on the S3 and backend layer, so any change carried more blast radius than was visible on the surface. After weeks of troubleshooting with the cloud architect, one major failure traced back to an extra, undocumented stage baked into the AI-generated API Gateway configuration that nobody knew existed. Separately, being new to SST, she initially masked a real deploy bug with a try-catch that worked locally but hid a legitimate failure once it reached dev (see [[sst-cdk-environment-assumption]]).

## Outcome
She worked closely with stakeholders to understand their existing document structure and access patterns, running weekly demos through the rebuild. Over about four and a half months, September 2025 to January 2026, she took DocHub from unrunnable to production-ready, preserving every dependency other teams already had on it. At the final demo, the stakeholder said, "This is excellent." Avenue One eliminated its Box subscription, saving an estimated $50K–75K a year. She shipped this just before being laid off in February 2026.

## Lessons Learned
The real risk in an AI-built codebase isn't necessarily code quality, it's lost reasoning. When a person writes code, some of that reasoning survives in comments or institutional memory. When a model writes it, the reasoning lived in a context window that closed the moment the session ended, leaving nothing behind to explain why something was built the way it was. This is why she distinguishes AI-assisted development, where a human directs the work, from AI-driven development, where the model is effectively the author.

## Future Evolution
AI-powered document organisation, retrieval, and structured output generation on top of DocHub (an actual LLM-driven layer, beyond OpenSearch metadata search) was on the roadmap but never built — the February 2026 layoff cut the project short before she got to it. The shipped system's search is OpenSearch metadata-only; Claude's confirmed role was as a coding tool during the rebuild, not a runtime feature. Do not describe DocHub as having a Claude-powered retrieval/organisation feature in any resume or content — that claim was caught and corrected 2026-08-24 after it had been sitting in the master resume (career/sindhuja-resume-current.md) and propagating into tailored resumes.

## AI Opportunities
The original build itself was the AI opportunity: an internal document platform built with Claude as the generation layer. The lesson that came out of inheriting it, that AI-driven codebases lose their reasoning once the session closes, is now a direct input into how she evaluates AI-generated code today.

title: job-agent — Personal AI Job-Matching Pipeline
body:
## Situation
Built a personal automation pipeline to handle her own job search instead of manually tracking postings — repo: github.com/sindhujaIBM/job-agent.

## Action
Architected as a Node.js 20 / TypeScript pipeline on the Serverless Framework (AWS Lambda, DynamoDB, SES, API Gateway), triggered daily by an EventBridge Scheduler:
- **job-scanner** pulls listings from documented public APIs and feeds only — We Work Remotely, Remote OK, Remotive, and Greenhouse/Lever endpoints for Calgary company career pages. Deliberately not scraping.
- **job-evaluator** scores each listing 0-10 against her resume/profile using Claude Haiku via AWS Bedrock.
- **job-notifier** sends a personalized email digest when real matches exist.
- **job-approver** handles her approval click, then triggers resume/cover-letter generation in a separate companion repository — generation is gated behind her manual approval, not fully automatic.

Explicitly chose to hand-build the orchestration in TypeScript rather than adopt an existing agent framework (LangChain/LangGraph), for direct control over workflow behavior — used live in a Clio interview mock as the "build" half of a build-vs-adopt answer, paired against the HQ LLM-evaluation story as the "adopt" half (see [[project_hq_model_eval]]).

## Outcome
Not yet confirmed — functional status, how long it's been running, and whether it's actually surfaced real applications/interviews all need to be asked directly.

## Learning
Not yet captured.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
A real, concrete "build vs. adopt" example on the build side — deliberately not using an existing agentic framework when control mattered more than speed. Pairs naturally with the HQ 4-LLM-provider evaluation as the "adopt" side of the same judgment call. Also a second, independent example of human-in-the-loop design discipline (approval gate before auto-generating/submitting anything) — same instinct as MaidLink's guardrails.

title: Kruthi — Coaching Tunnel Vision into Bird's-Eye View
body:
## Situation
Kruthi, a senior developer reporting to Sindhuja at Avenue One, expressed interest in becoming a team lead one day. Sindhuja started training her and giving her resources, but the real gap showed up in practice: on Scrum calls, when asked "do you think we'll make the deadline?", Kruthi would answer only from her own lane — "I don't know, I think my part will be done, I don't know about the rest of the team."

## Action
Sindhuja took her offline and explained the actual shift required: as a team lead, you need to see the bigger picture, not just your own piece — "you're not on the hook here, I am." She coached her on how to reframe the answer: state what she'd done, state what others were doing, assess whether collaborating on the connecting piece would make the deadline, and flag directly if it wouldn't. The next time Sindhuja asked the same kind of question, Kruthi answered that way — and kept improving at it over time, consistently answering from a bird's-eye view instead of the tunnel vision of a senior developer.

## Outcome
About six months in, Kruthi was ready to take on a minor project independently. Sindhuja gave her that responsibility and the autonomy to run it: Kruthi spoke directly to stakeholders, owned the initiative, and delivered it well.

## Learning
Developing someone into a leadership mindset isn't about resources or training alone — it's about catching the specific pattern (tunnel vision vs. bird's-eye view) in real, low-stakes moments (a Scrum standup question) and giving them language to practice the shift immediately, then giving real autonomy once the pattern holds.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: developing someone toward a role they don't yet have, balancing hands-on coaching with real delegated autonomy, and reading a specific behavioral gap (narrow answers vs. systemic awareness) rather than giving generic feedback. Use for: "tell me about developing someone on your team," "how do you balance autonomy and accountability when delegating," "describe coaching someone into a leadership mindset."

title: LinkedIn MCP Server
body:
## Situation
Needed a way to automate LinkedIn posting for personal social content (herself and Muni) as part of the content/growth workflow for MaidLink and their personal brands.

## Action
Built and compiled a working MCP (Model Context Protocol) server for LinkedIn (`tools/linkedin-mcp/`). Added two LinkedIn Developer App products deliberately scoped to what's actually needed now: "Share on LinkedIn" (personal posting via `w_member_social`) and "Sign In with LinkedIn" (person URN lookup). Explicitly deferred the Marketing Developer Platform product (needed for the MaidLink company page and analytics) because it's a gated, apply-and-wait product — not worth blocking on before personal posting is even working.

Later, published the server as a public npm package (`@sindhujaks/linkedin-mcp`) rather than leaving it a personal script. This meant removing what made it fast to build for one user: the original version pulled credentials from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store under hardcoded identity names (`sindhuja`, `muni`, `maidlink`), plus a fourth hardcoded identity for company-page posting. Rebuilt the credential layer around a `.env` file (`LINKEDIN_ACCESS_TOKEN`, `LINKEDIN_PERSON_URN`, optional `LINKEDIN_ORGANIZATION_URN`) and replaced the named identities with a generic `profile`/`company` role argument on each of the five tools (`post_to_profile`, `post_to_company_page`, `comment_on_post`, `get_recent_posts`, `get_post_analytics`), so the same server works for anyone, not just her. Hit a 403 ("two-factor authentication or a granular access token required") running `npm publish` at 2am — resolved in about ten minutes by enabling 2FA on the npm account.

## Outcome
Personal-account posting and cross-commenting work today. Company-page posting and analytics remain deferred until the gated access comes through.

Published `@sindhujaks/linkedin-mcp` v1.0.0 to npm. The next morning, Glama — an MCP server directory she'd never submitted to or heard of — had already auto-crawled the public GitHub repo (via its declared MCP SDK dependency) and scored it 4.1/5, unsolicited. Breakdown: perfect 5/5 on tool-naming clarity, tool-purpose disambiguation, and right-sized scope (five tools, not too many); the one deduction was for missing delete/update operations, which Glama's own note said aren't core to what the tool is for. Live at github.com/sindhujaIBM/linkedin-mcp, npmjs.com/package/@sindhujaks/linkedin-mcp, and glama.ai/mcp/servers/sindhujaIBM/linkedin-mcp.

## Learning
Sequencing matters when a dependency is gated and slow (apply-and-wait) versus self-serve — start with what's usable now, apply for the gated piece in parallel rather than blocking on it.

Publishing for a stranger turned out to be a legibility problem, not a cleverness problem — the LinkedIn integration code itself barely changed; what had to change was where credentials came from and whether someone with zero context could run it without asking her a question. An unsolicited, unprompted external score was independent confirmation that the scoping instinct (five clear tools, not twelve vague ones) reads as correct even to a system with no stake in the answer.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: a real, working MCP server built and deployed — a genuine technical credential for MCP-aware AI engineering roles. Frame as "built and deployed an MCP server for LinkedIn workflow automation" when relevant. Use for: "tell me about an MCP/tool-calling project," "describe a time you sequenced work around an external dependency," "tell me about a time your work got validated by someone outside your control," "how do you think about building for other people vs. just yourself."

title: MaidLink AI Estimator — Architecture and Cost
body:
## Business Problem
Homeowners want to know how much a cleaning job will cost before booking — the top source of anxiety in the transaction. Without an accurate estimate, pricing disputes and scope renegotiation break trust on both sides of the marketplace.

## Customer Problem
Two-sided: clients want a price before a cleaner shows up. Cleaning providers need the estimate calibrated to an efficient cleaner's pace, not an average one, or the business absorbs the gap between quote and reality.

## Technical Architecture
A client uploads photos of their space directly to S3 via a pre-signed URL (Lambda never touches the raw bytes) — confirmed directly by Sindhuja 2026-10-14, term added to match the mechanism already described here. Amazon Nova Lite on AWS Bedrock analyzes the photos and returns room-by-room cleaning time estimates, separate 1-cleaner and 2-cleaner hour figures, a full cleaning checklist, and coverage warnings when the photos don't fully capture the space. The upload pipeline itself runs through Lambda-layer security controls: JWT auth, rate limiting, PII-safe S3 key prefixes.

## Technologies
AWS Bedrock, Amazon Nova Lite, AWS Lambda, S3, JWT.

## Trade-offs

## Challenges
Not yet captured in detail — gap noted rather than invented.

## Outcome

title: OMS Re-platform Under Ambiguity and a Hostile Handover
body:
## Situation
Sindhuja was brought into Avenue One to lead the re-platforming of a legacy Order Management System off Unqork onto serverless AWS, with a 60-day deadline. She walked in with no laptop set up and no onboarding. Two specific gaps made it worse: she didn't know serverless or Lambda — her background was frontend and full-stack, not cloud architecture — and the senior engineer who had been the de facto lead before she arrived refused to tell her where the repo was or help her get set up. He had been running the team before the company brought her in to lead instead, and it showed immediately.

## Action
She didn't escalate the interpersonal friction — she worked around it. She went directly to business stakeholders, dug through the Unqork configuration herself, asked targeted questions of anyone willing to answer, and adjusted the architecture as she found gaps. She kept delivery visible and iterative so stakeholders always knew where things stood.

The reframe that made this workable: she didn't need to be the expert who wrote the code — she needed to be the person who made decisions and unblocked people. She treated it as a coordination problem, not a knowledge problem — the same way she'd approach any unfamiliar system. She coordinated constantly across infra, product, and QA, surfaced the real blockers, made scope and trade-off calls, and pushed decisions down to the team rather than being the bottleneck: what are the hard limits, what can we compromise on, what's non-negotiable.

## Outcome
The team delivered in 70 days against the original 60-day target. The system went live and the business migrated off Unqork. The 10-day slip was made explicit rather than hidden — what got cut, why it was the right trade-off, what would come back next quarter. She and the senior engineer ended up with a functional working relationship by the end of this phase (though the underlying dynamic resurfaced later — see related story).

## Learning
You can lead through real ambiguity by owning the decision-making and the coordination, even without domain expertise. Expertise is one path to credibility; clear decision-making under uncertainty is another. The team trusted her not because she knew Lambda, but because she knew how to unblock them, make trade-offs transparent, and push decisions to whoever had the context to make them.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: leading through ambiguity without technical seniority in the domain, working around interpersonal obstruction without escalating unnecessarily, and shipping under a hard deadline while being transparent about the miss. Use for: "tell me about a time you led without being the expert," "describe a delivery challenge," "how do you handle a difficult team dynamic," ambiguity/EM-round questions generally — swap in the specific company context per interview.

title: Prioritizing With No PM and No Specs
body:
## Situation
At MaidLink, Sindhuja has no product manager and no pre-defined specs. Everything that gets built, she decided was the right next thing.

## Action
Her system starts with what's blocking the business. The AI Estimator came first because it addressed the customer anxiety that couldn't be resolved manually — "how much is this going to cost me?" That had to be answered before the business could scale. Scheduling came next because it's the bottleneck holding back booking volume.

Within a sprint, the rule is simple: what's the highest-value item that's also ready? "Ready" means dependencies are resolved and the problem is defined well enough to build — she doesn't start something ambiguous just because it's high value; she does the discovery work first. When priorities conflict, she goes back to the customer: what does the person paying them need next.

## Outcome
A working prioritization system without a product function — decisions get made, sequenced, and revisited against real customer signal instead of a roadmap document.

## Learning
Prioritization without a PM isn't chaos if you have one consistent filter: business-blocking first, then highest-value-and-ready, then customer need as tiebreaker. The discipline is in refusing to start on high-value-but-undefined work just because it's tempting.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: product thinking without a formal product role, discipline around "ready" vs. "high value," and staying customer-anchored under ambiguity. Use for: "how do you prioritize," "tell me about working without a PM," founder/IC product questions.

title: Real-Time Over Daily Batch — DynamoDB Streams to Snowflake
body:
## Situation
During phase two of the Order Management System build at Avenue One, data needed to flow from the operational database into the functional reporting database. The operational DB was DynamoDB on AWS; the functional DB was Snowflake, queried by business users through a reporting tool called Sigma. The open question was sync frequency: once daily, or on every transaction.

## Action
Sindhuja built the pipeline using DynamoDB Streams feeding into Firehose to move data into Snowflake, and chose per-transaction (real-time) sync over daily batch. The driving reason was business need, not technical convenience: data up to twenty-four hours stale was leading business users to make the wrong calls. This wasn't an isolated choice — the same reasoning (real-time as the actual requirement wherever a business decision depends on current data, not a nice-to-have) led to implementing WebSockets elsewhere in the OMS SaaS platform too.

## Outcome
Business users had real-time data for decision-making instead of stale reports, directly improving the quality of calls made off that data.

## Learning
Evidence of a consistent architectural principle applied across a platform, not a one-off tactical fix — Sindhuja treats "does the business need current data to decide correctly" as the actual test, and answers it the same way wherever it shows up (streaming pipelines, WebSockets), rather than solving each instance in isolation.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: systems thinking (a repeatable principle, not an isolated decision), real-time architecture choices (DynamoDB Streams, Firehose), and tying a technical decision directly to business decision-quality. Use for: "tell me about a long-term architectural decision," "describe a technical choice with business impact," data pipeline / real-time architecture technical-depth questions. Distinct from [[oms-data-pipeline-ingestion-public]] (asset ingestion via webhooks replacing cron/Astronomer, 48hrs to under 5 min) — different pipeline, different decision, same company/project era.

title: Replacing Phone Calls and Excel with an OutSystems Mobile App for 800 Wells
body:
## Business Problem
Murphy Oil needed timely field data from roughly 800 wells for executive reporting, but the process depended on phone calls and Excel sheets with no enforced update cadence — if the person holding the data wasn't available, the report stalled.

## Customer Problem
Field staff had no fast way to report, and the executive team couldn't get timely, reliable aggregated data. Manual collation was slow and inconsistent.

## Technical Architecture
A mobile app built on OutSystems (a low-code, drag-and-drop platform) that fed data directly into a relational database, with reports generated automatically from that database instead of hand-assembled from scattered sources.

## Technologies
OutSystems — entirely new to Sindhuja at the time. Her prior background was JavaScript and Dojo, plus Visual Basic from school, which gave her a head start on OutSystems' drag-and-drop paradigm.

## Trade-offs
She couldn't force field staff to stop using Excel and phone calls outright — instead of mandating a process change, she made structured mobile data entry easy enough that it replaced the old habit on its own.

## Challenges
Learning an entirely unfamiliar low-code platform from scratch, single-handedly, within a roughly 10-month consulting engagement (via Hashmap/NTT Data).

## Outcome
Cut field reporting time from weeks to 48 hours. Executive reporting on well data moved from manual phone/Excel collation to automated generation off a relational database.

## Lessons Learned
Adjacent prior experience — Visual Basic's drag-and-drop model, from school — transferred faster into an unfamiliar platform than expected. Recognizing a transferable pattern speeds up learning genuinely new tools, even ones with no direct prior exposure.

## Future Evolution
Sindhuja moved on from Murphy Oil in February 2019; no further evolution captured here.

## AI Opportunities
Not discussed — this predates her AI-heavy work, consistent with the same era noted in other pre-2021 stories. Don't infer or backfill AI angles that weren't part of the actual project.

## Also at Murphy Oil (thinner detail — not full stories yet)
- **Enersight** — a separate initiative building an API between a relational database and Hadoop. Direction uncertain: she recalls it as relational DB → Hadoop (Hadoop ingesting the data), but wasn't fully sure; an earlier master-resume/timeline note described the pipeline as Hadoop → relational DB with downstream Power BI reporting. Not reconciled — don't assert either direction as confirmed without checking with her again.
- **Power BI reporting** — a separate, "minor" reporting project generating reports off existing data. Minimal detail captured so far; may or may not be the same reporting layer referenced in the Enersight note above.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: learning a genuinely unfamiliar technology from scratch and shipping real impact solo, recognizing transferable patterns across unrelated tools (Visual Basic → OutSystems), and solving a behavior-change problem through better tooling rather than mandate. Use for: "tell me about learning something new under pressure," "describe a time you shipped solo," "how do you handle resistance to a new process," technical-adaptability and ownership questions.

title: REST Over EventBridge — Matching Architecture to the Phase
body:
## Situation
Architecting a data pipeline at Avenue One, the team looked at the existing infrastructure — Sprockets was built on EventBridge — and naturally proposed using EventBridge here too, since it was already proven in the codebase.

## Action
Sindhuja stepped back and looked at the roadmap and timeline. For this specific phase, with a tight shipping window and limited scope, she made the case for something simpler: REST API calls, treated as a bridge between systems, rather than building out a full EventBridge orchestration layer the near-term scope didn't justify. She didn't decree it — she laid out the timeline, the roadmap, and the actual near-term need, and made the trade-off explicit to the team.

## Outcome
The team agreed. They built the pipeline with REST API calls; other systems functioned normally, and it worked exactly as intended. The simpler approach stayed the architecture — there was no later migration to EventBridge.

## Learning
Architecture isn't about picking the objectively "right" pattern in a vacuum — it's about matching the architecture to real constraints: timeline, roadmap, what's actually needed right now versus later. Over-engineering for a temporary state costs time and complexity you don't have yet. The team trusted the reasoning because the constraints were real and she owned the decision with them rather than imposing it.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: architectural judgment under time pressure, and the ability to talk a team out of the "proven" pattern when it's not the right fit for the current phase. Use for: "tell me about an architecture decision," "describe a time you guided a team toward a different technical direction," trade-off and technical-leadership questions.

title: Ron Kolias — Collective Ownership vs. Self-Preservation
body:
## Situation
Asked to describe the best engineer she's worked with, contrasted against someone else in her top five. Ron Kolias, at Avenue One, is the answer — not because of his technical output, but because of how he made people around him feel safe admitting what they didn't know.

## Action
What made Ron stand out: Sindhuja felt safe telling him she didn't understand something, because he explained complex things without a trace of ego — you walked away knowing more and feeling better, not smaller. She contrasts him with a second, technically capable engineer whose instinct under pressure was different: when something broke in production, his first move was to check whether the root cause touched his own PR, and step back once it didn't.

## Outcome
Ron's first move in the same situation was to help fix it — whose fault it was didn't enter into it. One operates from collective ownership, the other from self-preservation. Both can ship code; only one makes the team better while doing it.

For the second engineer, she didn't raise the pattern on the first incident — one data point could be anything. Once it became a pattern, she'd bring it up informally and reframe it around his own reality: the next time something breaks in prod, it might be his code, and he's going to need the team behind him. That reframe landed better than a conversation about team values would have.

## Learning
The engineers she most wants to hire and develop aren't the most technical by default — they're the ones who make everyone around them more capable without needing credit for it. That's a hiring and development signal as much as a technical one.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: what she actually values in engineering talent (psychological safety, collective ownership) versus surface technical strength, and a concrete coaching technique (reframe around self-interest rather than values-language) for engineers who default to self-preservation. Use for: "describe the best engineer you've worked with," "what do you look for in engineering talent," mentoring and team-culture questions.

title: Self-Initiated Security Audit — 13 Findings, All Remediated Before the Post Went Up
body:
## Situation
MaidLink had moved from a side project to a platform with real customers booking real cleanings, real maids getting paid, and real maids getting access to real homes. Nobody asked for a security audit — Sindhuja ran a full review of every service (auth, users, booking, admin, infrastructure) herself, unprompted, specifically because the stakes had become real rather than theoretical.

## Action
Thirteen findings, each remediated before the post describing them went up. The standout and most serious: an internal `devLogin` endpoint (built to skip Google OAuth during local testing — pass a UUID, get a signed JWT for that user) was supposed to be blocked in production by checking `process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'`. The actual production value, set by `serverless.yml`, was `prod`, not `production` — a one-character mismatch that meant the guard never fired. The endpoint had been live, unauthenticated, and reachable in production for two weeks before the audit caught it.

Other findings, by category:
- **Token lifetime**: JWT access tokens had a 24-hour TTL — reduced to 15 minutes, with silent background refresh so the user experience doesn't change but a stolen token's exposure window shrinks from a day to 15 minutes. Also added a minimum 32-character length check on `JWT_SECRET` (previously any non-empty string was accepted, making the HMAC-SHA256 signing key brute-forceable).
- **Token storage (XSS exposure)**: refresh tokens were returned in the JSON response body and stored in `localStorage`, readable by any JavaScript on the page — including injected code from an XSS vulnerability. Fixed by moving to an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookie, so the token is never readable by client-side JS even if XSS exists.
- **Race condition**: concurrent requests using the same refresh token could both pass the validity check before either revoked the other (a classic TOCTOU bug). Fixed with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` to lock the database row for the transaction's duration.
- **Over-broad IAM**: SES permissions had `Resource: '*'` (compromised Lambda credentials could send email as any identity in the account, not just maidlink.ca) — scoped to the specific SES identity ARN. S3 bucket CORS allowed `AllowedOrigins: ['*']` with PUT enabled (any website could initiate uploads) — restricted to the real domains plus localhost for dev.
- **Path traversal risk**: S3 upload keys were prefixed with a booking UUID, but the code only checked that the key *started with* the expected prefix, never validating that the UUID itself was actually UUID-shaped — leaving room for path-traversal characters to slip through. Fixed with a UUID regex validated before the key is constructed.
- **Information leakage via error codes**: three booking handlers returned `403 ForbiddenError` for bookings that existed but didn't belong to the requesting user — which lets an attacker enumerate valid booking IDs by distinguishing 403 (exists) from 404 (doesn't exist). Changed all three to `404 NotFoundError`: if you don't own it, it doesn't exist from your perspective.

## Outcome
All 13 findings remediated before the write-up was published. The audit also confirmed what was already solid: parameterized SQL everywhere (no injection risk), a 32-character Secrets-Manager-generated RDS password, the database in a private VPC with correctly scoped Lambda security group rules, CloudFront enforcing TLS 1.2+, and S3 public-access block fully enabled.

## Learning
The most serious bug wasn't a sophisticated exploit — it was a one-character string mismatch (`prod` vs `production`) that had been silently live for two weeks. Her own framing: these weren't hard problems, they were deferred problems, and the right moment to audit is before you have a reason to, not after a breach makes the deferral expensive. "Don't wait for a reason to audit. The reason is that you're live."

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: proactive, self-directed security ownership with no external mandate; real technical depth across multiple distinct vulnerability classes (auth bypass, token lifetime/storage, race conditions, IAM least-privilege, path traversal, information disclosure via error codes); and intellectual honesty about what was wrong, not just what was fixed. Use for: "tell me about a security audit you've run," "describe finding and fixing a serious vulnerability," "how do you think about security in a fast-moving startup," secure-coding and cybersecurity-governance questions generally. One of the strongest, most technically specific security stories in her history — self-initiated, pre-incident, not reactive.

title: Shipping AI Without a Mandate
body:
## Situation
AI wasn't on the official roadmap when Sindhuja joined Avenue One — she was hired to lead backend delivery and the OMS re-platform. But she saw a concrete opportunity where AI would replace manual work, not hypothetically: a buyer probability engine to score acquisition targets.

## Action
She brought a proposal to stakeholders to build the engine using OpenAI — a problem the business already had but hadn't connected to AI as a solution. She didn't ask for permission to prototype — she built a working version in a week and showed the output directly to the business team.

## Outcome
The conversation changed immediately once there was something real to look at. The buyer probability engine went into production on OpenAI.

## Learning
Leadership in that moment meant reading the business need correctly, building credibility with a working system instead of a slide deck, and taking the risk of building before anyone had officially sanctioned it.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: leading without a mandate, translating a business need into an AI solution nobody had asked for by name, and using a working prototype instead of a pitch to change minds. Use for: "tell me about a time you led without authority," "describe how you introduced AI into a business that wasn't asking for it," founder/innovation-angle questions.

title: SkillUp — Government of Alberta Labour Market Platform
body:
## Business Problem
Cybera, an Alberta-based not-for-profit delivering digital infrastructure for government, research, and public-sector innovation, needed to deliver SkillUp — a Government of Alberta funded labour market intelligence platform — under real ministry program requirements, compliance, and accessibility constraints. Confirmed via web search (2026-10-16): funded by the **Ministry of Jobs, Economy and Trade**, with initial support from the **Ministry of Advanced Education** (source: cybera.ca/skillup/). Sindhuja separately recalled this as "Ministry of Jobs" and connected it to the Ministry of Technology and Innovation being "carved out" of it — that carve-out (Oct 21, 2022) is already documented at the time this ministry was apparently named Jobs, Economy **and Innovation**, before being renamed. Whether "Jobs, Economy and Innovation" (pre-2022) and "Jobs, Economy and Trade" (current) are the same ministry lineage under a later rename, versus two distinct entities, has not been confirmed from a single source — this is Claude's own synthesis of two separately-sourced facts, not a verified single fact. Don't state the rename as settled in an interview; the safe, confirmed claim is just that SkillUp was GoA-funded and that Technology and Innovation was carved out of a ministry that also covered jobs/economy, in the same general lineage.

## Customer Problem
Albertans needed four things a fragmented labour market didn't provide: real-time occupations data (filtered by sector/location, with in-demand skills and certifications), a skills explorer for career-changers to identify transferable skills and training pathways, a regional employment tool for people considering relocating within Alberta (salary data by region), and an interests-based discovery tool — Career Safari — built on the O*NET interest model (RIASEC: Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional) to suggest occupations based on what someone actually enjoys, not just their existing resume. Confirmed directly from Cybera's own SkillUp page (cybera.ca/skillup), 2026-10-14 — the platform's own stated mission is "Putting Alberta's labour market data to work." Note: the public page lists SkillUp's full operational lifecycle as 2019–2025, wider than Sindhuja's own tenure (June 2021–May 2024) — the platform existed roughly two years before she joined and continued about a year after she left.

## Technical Architecture
Node.js/TypeScript backend, React frontend, a GraphQL API layer coordinating between data-science pipelines and the frontend, PostgreSQL for relational data, hosted on AWS Amplify and AWS Lightsail. High-throughput ingestion processed roughly 58,000 job advertisements daily, feeding three distinct public-facing services with different data models and user needs.

## Technologies
Node.js, TypeScript, React, GraphQL, PostgreSQL, AWS Amplify, AWS Lightsail, Jest, TestCafe, BrowserStack, Agile/Scrum. Infrastructure-as-code: originally **Terraform** while deployed on RAC (Cybera's own Rapid Access Cloud); rebuilt in **AWS CDK** when the team moved deployment to AWS mid-project, anticipating more traffic than RAC could handle (confirmed directly by Sindhuja, 2026-10-21).

## Trade-offs
GoA ministry stakeholders had specific program requirements but weren't technical — architecture had to be translated from policy language into something reliable and compliant without being over-engineered for the actual mandate.

## Challenges
High cross-system dependency between the data-science pipelines and the GraphQL layer; sustained 36-month delivery against evolving GoA program requirements across multiple releases; team coordination across engineers, data scientists, a dedicated UX designer, product ownership, and GoA ministry stakeholders, each with different delivery cadences and definitions of done.

A dedicated team of data scientists ran Jupyter notebooks to find patterns in the labour market data and apply machine learning for predictive analysis (e.g., transferable-skills pathways, regional employment trends). The dev team's job was taking that output and integrating it directly into the product's web page — a continuous, ongoing collaboration between data science and engineering, not a one-off handoff.

## Outcome
Delivered all three services at scale — roughly 58,000 job ads processed daily in real time. Sindhuja led all engineering delivery decisions as Technical Lead: architecture, tech stack, design patterns, code quality standards, plus facilitating Agile ceremonies and serving as the primary bridge between GoA stakeholders and the engineering team.

## Lessons Learned
Building trust with non-technical government stakeholders means translating requirements into architecture, not just implementing what's asked for literally. Team growth needs an explicit structure — not just "years at the company" — to actually retain people (see the mentorship story, related).

## Future Evolution
Sindhuja moved on from Cybera in 2024; no further evolution captured here.

## AI Opportunities
Not discussed in any source material for SkillUp specifically — this predates her AI-heavy AWS work. Don't infer or backfill AI angles that weren't part of the actual project.

## Team notes (not yet full stories — capture properly later)
Sindhuja mentored three engineers on this team: **Rulan** (frontend engineer who grew into UX/design and backend GraphQL work — see related story), **Jaide Porter** (joined later, single-handedly implemented one of the flows inside SkillUp — real, but only this one sentence of detail exists so far; surname confirmed 2026-10-21. Now at Clio, and is Sindhuja's referral contact there — see [[project_job_search]]), and **Derek** (joined alongside Jaide; no story detail captured yet). Don't expand Jaide's or Derek's notes into full narratives without more detail from Sindhuja directly.

title: The Avenue One Deal Lifecycle: OMS, the Data Pipeline, and Transaction Manager
body:
## Business Problem
Avenue One ran its entire deal lifecycle, sourcing through closing, on Unqork, an expensive, inflexible no-code platform. As tech lead responsible for eliminating Unqork, Sindhuja owned re-architecting the two core systems in that lifecycle, the Order Management System (OMS) and Transaction Manager (TM), onto modern serverless AWS, while retaining overall accountability for the third system in the same initiative, Property Management, which was rebuilt by someone else on her team.

## Customer Problem
Internally, this served several teams across Avenue One's real-estate acquisition business: the sourcing team needed a way to turn a cold-called seller into a tracked deal; the business needed a fast, data-driven way to identify likely buyers and value a deal so it could move quickly; and once a deal was won, title/closing partners and the accounting team needed a reliable system tracking each asset's exact state on the path to closing, so funds and title only released once everything checked out.

## Technical Architecture
Two distinct systems connected by a data pipeline she also built. **OMS**: AWS AppSync (GraphQL) + DynamoDB. A deal enters OMS once the sourcing team's cold-calling turns a seller into a live deal, sellers often have more than one property. Once a deal is in place, a buybox-based buyer probability prediction system (OpenAI API on AWS Lambda) and an AVM (Automated Valuation Model) run in parallel, generating structured signals used to identify and reach out to likely buyers. Buyers can bid on the full deal or a subset of assets within it. Once a bid is won, the data pipeline enriches related systems and moves the won asset(s) into Transaction Manager. **Transaction Manager**: AWS Lambda + Aurora RDS, a state machine tracking each asset from "under contract" through "inspection" to "ready to close." Title and closing partners verify title at that stage; once verified, the accounting team releases funds to close. After close, the asset routes to the Property Management product if it's an on-market deal and the buyer wants Avenue One's property management services, or directly to the buyer otherwise.

## Technologies
AWS AppSync, DynamoDB, Lambda, Aurora RDS (PostgreSQL), OpenAI API, Node.js/TypeScript.

## Trade-offs
OMS and Transaction Manager deliberately used different data stores, DynamoDB for OMS versus Aurora RDS for Transaction Manager, rather than standardizing on one database across both systems. The specific reasoning behind that split wasn't captured in detail, noted as a gap rather than invented.

## Challenges
Coordinating a single asset's state reliably across three separate systems (OMS, the pipeline, Transaction Manager) and multiple internal/external parties (sourcing team, buyers, title and closing partners, accounting) without losing track of where it was in the lifecycle. Multi-property deals added real complexity, since buyers could win a subset of a deal rather than the whole thing, meaning the pipeline had to split and route individual assets rather than treating a deal as one atomic unit.

## Outcome
OMS shipped in 70 days (against a 60-day target). Transaction Manager shipped in roughly 3 months. Property Management was rebuilt separately by someone else on her team, under the same Unqork-elimination initiative. Combined, eliminating Unqork across all three systems saved Avenue One approximately $650K/year in platform fees, savings she was accountable for as the tech lead who owned the overall initiative, even though she did not personally build Property Management.

## Lessons Learned
Not yet captured in detail, gap noted rather than invented.

## Future Evolution
Not yet captured in detail, gap noted rather than invented.

## AI Opportunities
The buybox-based buyer prediction system and the AVM underwriting running in parallel at deal-entry are the clearest existing AI integration point in this lifecycle, already shipped, not hypothetical.

title: The Dog Scratch That Got MaidLink Bonded and Insured
body:
## Situation
In early 2025, before MaidLink had an app, back when the business ran on phone calls and Excel, one of the maids got a small scratch from a dog while on a cleaning job. The dog was playful, not aggressive, so the injury itself was minor.

## Action
The incident forced a harder question than the scratch itself: what if it hadn't been a playful dog? What if the maid had been seriously injured instead? That fear is what pushed Sindhuja and Muni to get MaidLink properly bonded and insured, through The Co-operators, well before the app existed.

## Outcome
MaidLink became a bonded and insured business while it was still just phone calls and a spreadsheet. That coverage is now a real trust signal for customers letting workers into their homes, not something added later for appearances.

## Learning
The gap between "small scratch" and "seriously injured" was luck, not risk management. A minor incident is a warning, not a relief. Waiting for the serious version of something to actually happen before getting covered isn't a plan, it's betting on luck holding.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
This is direct, lived experience being on the insured/bonded side of a compliance relationship, not just evaluating or vetting others (contrast with the Avenue One builder-database and RBAC stories, which are about vetting others). Strong for questions about risk management, trust and safety, or founder judgment under real stakes, and directly relevant to compliance-adjacent roles like the Tough Leaf/ClearComply interview that surfaced it.

title: The Hiring Call She Got Right But Couldn't Win
body:
## Situation
Cybera's team dynamic was junior and mid-level engineers who solved problems by talking things through openly — collaborative, and only workable if people were receptive to feedback. They were hiring for a senior engineering role, and a candidate came through who was technically very strong but, in the interview loop, didn't take feedback well: when challenged on a decision, he'd defend and explain why his way was right instead of exploring the question.

## Action
Sindhuja flagged this directly to her manager, specific about the behavior and why it mattered for this particular team: "Technically he's solid, but my team isn't equipped to handle someone who doesn't absorb feedback. They solve problems through dialogue, and that only works if everyone's receptive. This person will create friction. Hiring him risks breaking the collaboration model that makes this team effective."

## Outcome
He got hired anyway — the hiring manager prioritized technical strength. Ninety days in, her manager started noticing the team was always on their phones, avoiding 1-on-1s. They'd gone defensive because they couldn't engage with him directly — he'd just prove his point instead of exploring theirs. They had to let him go.

## Learning
She was right about the fit, but she didn't frame it in a way that could override the business decision. She should have come in with more specifics from the start — not just "I observed this in the loop" but the exact mechanism of how it breaks the collaboration model, and what it would cost the team, in terms concrete enough to compete with "he's technically strong." The deeper lesson: culture fit isn't soft, it's structural. If a team's engine is feedback loops and collaborative problem-solving, hiring someone who rejects feedback breaks the engine — that's a technical risk, not a personality judgment. She learned to document those observations in real time and be louder about them earlier in the process.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: hiring judgment, willingness to disagree with a hiring manager, and — just as important — honest reflection on being right but not persuasive enough. Use for: "tell me about a hiring decision you disagreed with," "describe a time you were overruled," "how do you evaluate culture fit," any question probing self-awareness after being proven correct.

title: The Try-Catch That Hid a Real Bug
body:
## Situation
Building DocHub, the document management system she inherited at Avenue One, the infrastructure-as-code was written in SST (Serverless Stack) — new to her, as was managing production infrastructure at that scale. The first local deploy failed: some resources tried to be created but already existed.

## Action
She read it as an idempotency issue and wrapped the failure in a try-catch. Tested locally — the second run worked perfectly. Confident it was solved, she moved it to the dev environment and deployed.

## Outcome
It failed immediately in dev. The error she'd wrapped was now swallowing legitimate failures, because dev's infrastructure model was completely different: the CDK stack there gets deleted and recreated on every deploy — it's not idempotent. The try-catch was looking for pieces that would never exist, and it hid the real problem instead of solving it.

## Learning
She'd made an assumption based on local behavior without understanding how the deployment pipeline actually worked — local and dev environments have fundamentally different infrastructure patterns, and behavior doesn't carry across. Now, before adding a workaround, she asks how the system actually behaves in the target environment and what the deployment model is, and tests there — not just locally. Infrastructure assumptions hide bugs: it's easy to fix something locally and think it's done, but without understanding the deployment model, a fix can mask the problem instead of solving it.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: learning from a real production-adjacent mistake, and a specific, transferable principle (don't assume environment parity; verify the deployment model before adding error-handling workarounds). Use for: "tell me about a time you failed," "describe a mistake and how you handled it," infrastructure/DevOps technical-depth questions.

title: TRC Garlands — Configurator-First Website Rebuild
body:
## Situation
TRC Garlands is her husband Muni's Calgary garland-making business — real, currently running on manual process. She's rebuilding it as a configurator-first website, on her own account (github.com/sindhujaIBM/trc-garlands), not as paid employment but as a real side build.

## Action
Wrote the full design doc suite first — product/UX, configurator spec, pricing engine, data + API, AWS + CMS, AI roadmap — before writing code. Chose AppSync GraphQL + DynamoDB for the backend, picking GraphQL over REST deliberately when the question came up. Deliberately followed MaidLink's component organization for the Next.js App Router structure, but not its visual palette — reusing a working pattern without reusing a brand.

## Outcome
Full design doc suite committed and pushed as of July 2026; code scaffolding is the next phase, not yet built.

## Learning
Not yet captured — revisit once the build itself is further along.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: building for someone else's real business (not just her own), architecture decision-making outside of paid work (GraphQL over REST, chosen deliberately), and reusing a proven component pattern without copying the brand. Use for: side-project/personal-build questions, "tell me about something you built outside of work."

title: When AI Is the Coder, the Architecture Is Still Yours
body:
## Situation
Working with Claude to build production systems (at Avenue One and at MaidLink), Sindhuja noticed the real skill shift wasn't in how she wrote prompts.

## Action
It was in holding the architectural vision the AI couldn't hold for her. Before AI touches a system, she has to already know what that system should look like — the direction, the review, the course-correction. That's the part that doesn't get automated away.

## Outcome
A working principle for how she builds with AI day to day: she stays the architect regardless of who's writing the code.

## Learning
The hardest part of building with AI isn't the prompting — it's the architecture. Claude doesn't know what the system should look like; she does. That's the job that shifted, not away, but toward.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: a genuine, lived perspective shift on what her value is when AI writes code — directly relevant to any "how has AI changed how you work" or "what's the future of engineering roles" question, and a credible AI-builder angle for content and interviews alike. Use for: AI-philosophy questions, "how do you use AI in your work," thought-leadership content.

title: When File-Level Permissions Stopped Working at 200K Documents
body:
## Situation
DocHub, the internal document intelligence platform Sindhuja inherited and rebuilt at Avenue One (a secure, serverless, VPC-only internal document system, later scaling past 200,000 documents), started with file-level access controls — permissions set per document.

## Action
As the document count grew, file-level ACLs became unmanageable fast. She replaced them with role-based access control: three tiers implemented via Auth0 — User (view-only), Manager (view + upload), Admin (view + upload + delete).

## Outcome
A permission model that scaled with the organization instead of the file count.

## Learning
Access control design should follow how people actually work, not how files happen to be organized. File-level granularity feels precise early on, but it doesn't scale with volume — role-based design does, because roles map to how an organization actually operates.

## Why This Matters (retrieval angle)
Evidence of: recognizing when an early technical choice stops scaling, and redesigning access control as a product decision, not just a security one. Use for: security/architecture technical-depth questions, "tell me about a system you had to redesign as it scaled," "describe an access-control or permissions decision." Same underlying platform as [[inherited-codebase-nobody-could-run]] (the inheritance/ownership angle) and [[dochub-architecture-deep-dive]] (the full system design) — this is the access-control lens on it.
